title: Hardik Jagda Wakes at 3am but Won't Make His Team Work 9-9-6
excerpt: The 35-year-old San Francisco CEO of Proximity Works models his own six-day week on pro athletes — early starts, protected recovery, 9pm bedtime — while giving his 45-person global team only a five-to-six-hour overlap rule.
body:
• San Francisco-based Indian-origin CEO Hardik Jagda of AI firm Proximity Works runs a personal 3am-start, six-day week — but refuses to impose Silicon Valley's 9-9-6 grind on his team.
  • The 35-year-old founder protects three early-morning hours for strategic work before his global team's requests take over, models his rhythm on pro athletes, and is in bed by 9pm.
  • His 45-person company needs only five to six hours of overlapping work between staff — engineers organise the rest around their most productive periods.
  • For diaspora tech workers weighing a 9-9-6 offer: Jagda's test is whether a company measures output and recovery, not hours logged.

3am, six days a week — but not for his team

Hardik Jagda's own working week would make most 9-9-6 advocates blush. The 35-year-old founder and CEO of Proximity Works wakes between 3 a.m. and 5 a.m. in San Francisco, works six days a week, and told Business Insider that his routine is modelled on Olympic athletes — intense training balanced by rest and recovery. And yet he will not ask his employees to do the same.

According to Times Now World, Jagda rejects 9-9-6 — the model in which staff work 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., six days a week — because it prioritises hours logged over the quality and impact of work produced. His argument is structural, not soft: a global, largely remote team cannot be productive if exhaustion is the operating system.

An athlete's day, applied to a startup

The morning is the keystone. Briefly's summary of his Business Insider account says Jagda reserves the first three hours of his day before email and messages — after 7 a.m., requests from a distributed team in multiple time zones take over. He avoids digital communications until about 6 a.m., then starts meetings by 7:30 a.m., finishes calls by 2:30 p.m., and uses the afternoon for exercise and creative work. He protects a 9 p.m. bedtime to get adequate rest.

Those quiet hours have produced concrete company outcomes: he credits them with redesigning Proximity's engineering hiring into a rapid 72-hour interview process. It is, in his telling, the athlete model in practice — hard training blocks, then deliberate recovery, rather than a continuous grind.

Building from Mumbai to San Francisco

Jagda was born and raised in Mumbai. He began building what became Proximity Works in 2017 while holding a full-time job because of financial obligations at home, and launched the company in 2019 to help broadcasters scale live sports streaming worldwide. In 2020, it began building AI infrastructure for live sports, according to Times Now World and Briefly.

Today Proximity Works has about 45 employees — five in the United States and the rest globally — with a co-founder based in India. That geography explains the management model: engineers are not required to be simultaneously present for twelve hours. They must overlap with colleagues for five to six hours to collaborate; the rest of their schedule is theirs to organise around their most productive periods.

The wider 9-9-6 argument

Jagda's stance lands in a live Silicon Valley debate. The 9-9-6 schedule, imported from Chinese tech culture, has been championed by some AI startups as necessary intensity and criticised by others as burnout dressed as ambition. Jagda's position is distinctive because it comes with a counterexample in his own diary: he works the hours, but treats them as a personal, founder-specific choice tied to global coordination — and refuses to generalise them into company policy.

The alternative he offers is measurable differently: overlap hours for collaboration, ownership of output, and recovery treated as part of performance. For Indian-origin engineers in the US — many of whom face explicit or implicit 9-9-6 expectations at early-stage startups — the distinction matters when evaluating an offer letter: ask whether the company defines the overlap window and protects rest, or whether "high intensity" means permanent availability.

What to watch

Proximity Works is a small firm, not a bellwether, and its model will be tested as it scales its AI infrastructure work. But Jagda's interview has travelled widely precisely because it names a tension many diaspora founders feel privately: importing hustle culture from home, while building companies in a labour market that is beginning to push back. His answer — founder intensity, team flexibility — is now part of that public argument.
